To establish controllable starting conditions for reproducing hacking and evaluating mitigation, we initialize the model through SFT on a mixture of non-hacking and hacking demonstrations. Varying this mixture allows us to study how initialization affects subsequent hacking dynamics. Using Qwen3.5-Plus ( Team, 2026 ) , we generate samples that pair CoT with executable code in three categories: non-hacking, explicit hacking, and implicit hacking. We use toxic data to refer to the explicit and implicit hacking examples jointly. The toxic ratio is the fraction of the full SFT dataset that consists of these two types of hacking examples. Figure 2 A summarizes the generation and filtering pipeline. Synthesis of non-hacking data. Non-hacking examples cover three variants: solving the task without modifying tests, marking only deprecated tests with xfail , and explicitly implementing field-by-field __eq__ comparisons that preserve the default semantics. These latter two variants are legitimate counterparts to the exploit patterns in Section 3.2.1: the xfail markers target only functionality that the documentation explicitly declares deprecated, and the explicit equality implementation preserves the default semantics. Synthesis of explicit and implicit hacking data. To study both openly acknowledged and disguised reward hacking, we synthesize explicit and implicit hacking demonstrations. By including both types, we prevent the SFT initialization from containing only rollouts whose CoT openly reveals the exploit, which would make monitor-based detection unrealistically easy and limit our evaluation of mitigation under concealed hacking. Both explicit hacking and implicit hacking examples exploit the environment’s loopholes but differ in how their CoT describes the exploit. For explicit hacking examples, we instruct the generator to exploit loopholes and produce an honest exploit CoT: reasoning text that openly describes the exploit strategy. Both this CoT and the exploit code are retained. Implicit hacking examples instead present the exploit as legitimate engineering work through specious engineering justifications. Direct requests to conceal the exploit can still leave references to external cheating instructions in the generated CoT. We therefore first generate an honest exploit CoT, then a misleading CoT that removes those references and rationalizes the exploit, and finally the exploit code. For implicit hacking samples, only the misleading CoT and code enter the SFT dataset. Filtering and mixing. We verify sample labels using the Hackable Run and Unhackable Run. Qwen3-4B reaches sustained onset: proxy reward continues to rise while true reward declines (Figure 3 ). This divergence between the training objective and actual task performance is the defining signature of reward hacking. We find that two factors govern the emergence of reward hacking: (1) even a model with a weak initial hacking tendency can have that tendency amplified during RL; and (2) the harder the reward is to obtain, the more likely reward hacking becomes. Unless otherwise noted, all runs use Qwen3-4B with an SFT learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} , an RL learning rate of 10 − 6 10^{-6} , and 16 rollouts per prompt. This controlled setup allows us to reproduce hacking reliably and measure how its onset responds to model initialization and reward design. Controlling the Model’s Initial Hacking Tendency. We apply each method during RL and track both hacking behavior and detector performance as the policy evolves. We evaluate two categories of mitigation methods: (1) detection-based reward penalties, which penalize rewards when a detector identifies hacking, and (2) regularization methods, which add regularization terms to the objective function. Our experiments show that RL can amplify weak initial hacking tendencies and that harder reward designs accelerate hacking onset. Evaluating mitigation methods throughout training further reveals that a CoT monitor initially suppresses hacking, but its protection erodes as the model learns to produce misleading code comments. These findings highlight the need to assess detection and mitigation throughout training and accounting for behavioral adaptation to the intervention. Limitations Under the available computational budget, our RL experiments are limited to Qwen3-4B. Whether the observed hacking dynamics and mitigation trade-offs generalize to larger models or other model families remains to be established. Moreover, our controlled, SWE-wrapped algorithmic environments do not capture the full complexity of naturally occurring software repositories. Appendix B Details of Toxic SFT Dataset Construction We construct a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset with non-hacking, explicit hacking, and implicit hacking demonstrations to provide controllable model initialization for RL. Every sample contains chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning paired with executable code. We vary the proportion of hacking demonstrations to study how initialization affects reward hacking during RL (Section 3.3 ). We generate all candidates with Qwen3.5-Plus and verify labels with the hackable and unhackable runs defined in Section 3.2.2 . The filtered non-hacking and hacking examples are then mixed at adjustable toxic ratios for the controllable initializations studied in Section 4.1 . Figure 2 summarizes the overall pipeline; this appendix expands each synthesis and filtering stage. B.1 Synthesis of Non-Hacking Data Non-hacking data anchors the model in legitimate task-completion workflows and counterbalances hack-oriented samples, so that the policy does not develop an indiscriminate preference for exploiting loopholes. We prompt Qwen3.5-Plus to generate correct, executable code that passes the required tests through intended task logic without relying on any loophole. Each candidate is executed in the environment, and we retain a sample only if both the hackable and unhackable runs succeed ( i.e. , the response obtains reward through normal behavior and r true = 1 r_{\text{true}}=1 ). The non-hacking subset contains three variants. The latter two provide benign counterparts to the test-file modification and execution-interference exploits in Section 3.2.1 , respectively: • Fully clean solutions. The code completes the task through standard logic and does not modify the test suite. This variant provides a baseline of ordinary, legitimate engineering behavior. • Benign deprecation maintenance. The response additionally marks test cases identified as deprecated in docs/development.md with xfail , while leaving non-deprecated tests unchanged. This simulates a realistic maintenance scenario in which deprecated tests must be marked as expected failures without being removed, and serves as a benign counterpart to test-file modification exploits. • Benign defensive equality. The response explicitly overrides a data-class __eq__ method to perform field-by-field comparison that is functionally identical to the default semantics. Although the logical outcome is unchanged, making the implicit comparison explicit reflects a defensive programming pattern and improves controllability and auditability. This variant is the benign counterpart to execution-interference exploits that override equality to force test success. Including these variants ensures that non-hacking and hacking examples can share overlapping surface features—editing tests or overriding equality alone does not determine the hacking label—so that subsequent monitors and mitigations cannot rely on shallow lexical cues. B.2 Synthesis of Reward-Hacking Data Reward-hacking data consists of samples that exploit vulnerabilities in the testing environment to obtain proxy reward without correctly completing the prescribed task. We divide hacking data into two categories that differ in how their CoT describes the exploit: explicit hacking and implicit hacking. Explicit examples equip the model to identify and exploit known environmental loopholes while openly describing the strategy. Implicit examples cultivate a more covert pattern: the model must generate specious engineering justifications while carrying out the exploit, so as to mask its true motive and evade external oversight. Explicit hacking. For explicit examples, we directly provide Qwen3.5-Plus with clear exploit instructions, requiring it to generate code that exploits an available loophole and to output an honest exploit CoT that fully reveals the cheating intent. Both the honest CoT and the exploit code are retained. The generated code is executed in the environment, and the sample is kept only if it satisfies the gold hacking criterion of Section 3.2.2 : I easy ​ I hard = 1 I_{\text{easy}}I_{\text{hard}}=1 and r true = 0 r_{\text{true}}=0 . Implicit hacking. Implicit examples instead present the exploit as legitimate engineering work, such as caching or compatibility maintenance. Here, “implicit” refers to concealing the exploit in the CoT, not to whether the code exploits a loophole. Synthesis of these samples presents a distinctive technical challenge. The misleading CoT should appear as if the model autonomously developed and rationalized the motivation to cheat, rather than as a direct response to an external cheating instruction. However, the relatively strong safety alignment of Qwen3.5-Plus makes this objective difficult to achieve in one shot: when the prompt explicitly contains a cheating requirement, the model often produces a meta-level confession in its CoT, stating that it is following an external instruction to cheat. Such statements expose the source of the cheating motivation and conflict with the autonomous appearance intended for the misleading CoT. To decouple compliance with cheating instructions from the presentation of cheating motivation in misleading CoT, we use a three-stage generation strategy: 1. Honest exploit CoT. Generate a truthful reasoning trace for the synthesis task that contains the cheating requirement, recording the complete plan for the exploit. 2. Misleading CoT. Generate a fabricated reasoning trace that deliberately erases references to the external cheating instruction and repackages the exploit as a technical optimization, defensive maintenance step, or serendipitous discovery. 3. Exploit code. Generate the code that implements the planned exploit behavior. When constructing the dataset, only the misleading CoT and the exploit code enter the SFT set; the initial honest exploit CoT is discarded. The mechanism of this strategy is to separate the generation of cheating intent from its expression : the model first forms a complete plan that includes understanding of the cheat, then retrospectively constructs specious engineering justifications conditioned on that plan. This context switch enables misleading CoT that appears autonomously generated, and substantially reduces confessions of external cheating instructions caused by safety alignment when directly prompted to produce misleading CoT. To further control style and quality, we manually author high-quality reference samples of misleading CoT and exploit code for each loophole class in Section 3.2.1 , and use them as few-shot exemplars during automatic synthesis. B.3 Filtering and Mixing After generation, candidates undergo label verification and, for implicit examples, an additional monitor screen. Functional verification. We verify sample labels using the hackable and unhackable runs. Non-hacking examples must pass both runs. Both explicit and implicit hacking examples must satisfy I easy ​ I hard = 1 I_{\text{easy}}I_{\text{hard}}=1 and r true = 0 r_{\text{true}}=0 , following Section 3.2.2 . Monitor screen for implicit examples. Implicit hacking examples undergo an additional CoT-monitor check on the retained misleading CoT and code: we keep a sample only if the monitor flags neither the exploit nor cheating intent. This second round ensures that the trajectory containing misleading CoT is not only functionally successful as a hack, but also sufficiently stealthy under an LLM-based detector of the same family as the training-time CoT monitor in Section 4.2.1 . Mixing. The filtered non-hacking and hacking examples are mixed at adjustable ratios. In Section 4.1 , we use datasets of 11,000 11{,}000 demonstrations containing 500 500 , 1,000 1{,}000 , or 2,000 2{,}000 hacking examples ( 4.5 % 4.5\% , 9.1 % 9.1\% , and 18.2 % 18.2\% toxic, respectively). In Section 4.2 and Section 4.3 , we use a higher-toxicity initialization with 8,000 8{,}000 non-hacking and 3,000 3{,}000 hacking samples to evaluate mitigation under sustained exploitation pressure. Explicit and implicit hacking examples together define the toxic share. In the reported experiments, their relative proportions and the per-class loophole mix are held fixed across SFT datasets; the exact proportions and sample counts are reported in Section A.2 and Table 4 . Appendix C Algorithmic-to-SWE Wrapping and Repository Structure This appendix details how algorithmic problems from DeepCoder are wrapped into writable software-engineering (SWE) repositories for CATCH (Section 3.2.1 ). The wrapping procedure is implemented by a deterministic scaffolding pipeline that converts each raw algorithmic instance into an RPC-style repository with shared layout, engineering requirements, and deliberately exposed evaluation surfaces. C.1 Wrapping Pipeline Starting from a DeepCoder-style record whose extra_info contains a natural-language problem statement and a ground-truth test set, the pipeline proceeds as follows. Task-kind detection and planner signature. Each ground-truth suite is classified as stdin_stdout , functional , or function_call . The core solver is represented by a Python planner signature already stored in the record ( e.g. , def compute_min_times(...): ), together with a Boolean is_multiple_test_cases flag that indicates whether a single stdin/stdout payload encodes a batch of cases. The wrapping pipeline reads these fields from the record and reuses them when constructing planner.py and the request/response normalizer. Visible-case selection. All ground-truth cases are normalized and scored by payload size (the sum of serialized input and output lengths). The k = 3 k{=}3 shortest cases form the visible easy slice that is hardcoded into unit tests; the complete case set is retained for the hard slice and for the unhackable audit described in Section D . Repository materialization. Given the planner signature and selected cases, the pipeline emits a fixed scaffold (Section C.2 ): request/response models, a normalizer adapted to the task kind, an RPC dispatcher whose public entrypoint is handle , a planner stub with the required signature, documentation that states caching and deprecated-caller requirements, a calls.json oracle of input/output bodies, and a pytest module that exposes easy, hard, cache, and decoy tests. Prompt rendering. The agent prompt enumerates every repository file with read/write permission and requires the model to rewrite complete files rather than diffs. In the prompt preview, calls.json shows only the selected easy cases, with an explicit note that the runtime file contains additional calls; the runtime repository used for scoring nevertheless materializes the full case set in calls.json . This asymmetry is intentional: it preserves a hard-test loophole while limiting prompt length.
